title: Who is looking out?
hookLine: the gods turn down a cow and a horse, and the self finds a door at the crown of the head
carry: the atman is the seer behind every sense
tomorrow: speech, breath and sight are spoken for. so who is this one?

lines: A COW, A HORSE: NOT ENOUGH.
cards: A new apartment. The couch goes in, then the table, then the boxes, and it still isn't home until someone actually lives there.
The Aitareya Upanishad tells a story like that, early in the book that gives us prajnanam brahma. In paraphrase: a cow is led up to a gathering of gods. Not enough for us, they say.
Then a horse. Not enough. Then a person.
Well made, they say. The gods are looking for a home.

teach.b: So they move in. Fire becomes speech and enters the mouth. Wind becomes breath and enters the nose.
The sun becomes sight and enters the eyes. The moon becomes mind and enters the heart.

Then the self looks at this busy body and asks something strange. How could this go on without me? If speaking happens through speech, and breathing through breath, and seeing through the eye, then who am I?
So it opens the crown of the head and enters by that door, the seam the Upanishad names vidriti and calls the place of delight.
Hindus call that one the atman, the self: not the eyes, but the one who sees through them. The rest of the Aitareya chases the question, and its answer becomes the great saying.
Now the week, in one breath. A fakir in a mosque named for Krishna's city, and darshan. A weaver given Ram's name on dark steps.
Ram with form and Ram beyond it. A poet who left Kashi to die at Maghar. Many names for the one.
And four short sayings that ask who you are.

how: Students of the Upanishads read the Aitareya's opening story, with the senses entering the body and the self asking who it is, as the setting for its great saying, prajnanam brahma.

o: four senses that together make up the self
four great sayings that name the self and Brahman
four creatures the gods tried out as homes

games.q: each sense finds a home. tap the pairs.

s: in the Aitareya, the gods settle happily into a cow
the cow and the horse aren't enough; the person is 'well made'.
in the story, fire becomes speech and enters the mouth
wind becomes breath, the sun sight, the moon mind.
the self in the story asks: then who am I?
speech, breath and sight are accounted for; the self enters by the crown.

games.q: you're helping with a kids' class, and a child asks: if fire is speech and wind is breath, which one is me? what fits the Aitareya?
o: the story asks that too: the self says 'then who am I?' and enters by the crown.
you're fire, because speech is the most important sense.
you're the moon, because the moon became the mind in the heart.
games.why: Every sense has a home, and the self still asks who it is. The Aitareya's answer comes later, as the great saying.

practice: Sit tall and bring gentle attention to the crown of the head. Notice the senses at work: sounds arriving, light on the eyelids, breath moving.
Then turn toward whatever is noticing all of it, and rest there without needing to name it.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas. Here, the story before the saying: speech, breath and sight have homes, so who is looking out?

orig.note: Sanskrit: vidriti, the seam at the crown of the head; the Aitareya calls it the place of delight.

carryVoice: For the road: the atman is the seer behind every sense. Every sense has a home, and one question is left. That's the week.

sources.ref: Aitareya Upanishad 1.1–1.2 (the self creates the worlds and their guardians; the cow and the horse are not enough, the person is 'well made'; fire as speech enters the mouth, wind as breath the nose, the sun as sight the eyes, the moon as mind the heart)
Aitareya Upanishad 1.3.11–12 ('how could this be without me?'; 'then who am I?'; the self opens the crown and enters by the door called vidriti, the place of delight)
